title: Java Introduction
learningObjectives: Define Java as a general-purpose, class-based programming language.
Explain the roles of Java source code, bytecode and the Java Virtual Machine.
Describe what platform independence means and identify its compatibility limits.
Recognize the class and main method in a basic Java application.
Identify common Java application areas without confusing the language with a framework.

understand.concept: Java is a high-level, general-purpose, class-based programming language. Developers write source code in `.java` files. A Java compiler translates valid source into class files containing bytecode. A compatible Java Virtual Machine (JVM) loads and executes that bytecode in a target environment.
understand.whyItMatters: Understanding the source-to-bytecode-to-JVM path explains how Java applications are built, why a JDK is needed for development and why a compatible runtime is needed to execute compiled programs.
understand.analogy: Source code is like instructions written for a translator; bytecode is a standardized intermediate form; the JVM is the runtime that understands and executes that form.
understand.analogyLimit: Bytecode does not make every program automatically portable. Programs may depend on operating-system features, native libraries, runtime versions, file paths or external services.

explain.narrative:
## Java as a language

Java is class-based and supports object-oriented programming. It also includes primitive types, expressions, control statements, methods, packages and a large standard library.

## From source to execution

1. Write source code in a `.java` file.
2. Use the Java compiler (`javac`) to compile the source.
3. The compiler produces `.class` files containing Java bytecode.
4. A compatible JVM loads the class files and executes the program.

The JDK provides development tools such as `javac`; runtime components provide the JVM and libraries required to run applications.

## Platform independence

Java bytecode can run on different systems when a compatible JVM and required libraries are available. Portability still depends on avoiding or adapting platform-specific assumptions such as native code, file-system differences and environment configuration.

questions.prompt: What does javac produce from a successfully compiled Java source file?
questions.explanation: The Java compiler normally writes class files containing bytecode.
The JVM loads and executes Java bytecode.

questions.prompt: Which file extension is commonly used for Java source code?
questions.explanation: Java source files conventionally use the .java extension.

questions.prompt: What is a realistic meaning of Java portability?
options: Bytecode can run where a compatible JVM and required libraries exist
Every program behaves identically on every device
Java programs never use platform features
questions.answer: Bytecode can run where a compatible JVM and required libraries exist
questions.explanation: Portability depends on runtime compatibility and program dependencies.

questions.prompt: Which item is a Java language feature rather than a framework?
questions.explanation: Classes are part of the Java language.
